newsitem.title: USA: Panel votes to ban U.S. funds for assisted suicide.
newsitem.headline: Panel votes to ban U.S. funds for assisted suicide.

text.p: A House subcommittee Tuesday approved legislation barring use of federal funds for assisted suicide, bringing Congress into the emotionally charged debate over the right to die.
The full House Commerce Committee is expected to vote on the bill next week, which would prevent use of Medicaid, Medicare or other federal money for expenses involved with physician-aided suicide.

"This bill achieves only one objective -- but it is a very important objective -- the assurance that federal tax dollars will not be used to assist in the suicide of any American," said Commerce health subcommittee chairman Mike Bilirakis, a Florida Republican.

The bill, approved by voice vote, does not ban or restrict assisted suicide, nor prohibit use of state or private money to pay for it. Opponents of the measure said Congress was addressing a problem that did not exist.
California Representative Henry Waxman, a Democrat, said the bill's only underlying purpose was "to make a statement, because we're not funding any physician-aided suicides (now)."
He called the bill "redundant, a mere restatement of the status quo."
The Supreme Court earlier this year heard arguments in a landmark legal case supporters hope will establish a constitutional right to die. A decision is expected this summer.
More than 35 states have outlawed assisted suicide. Oregon voters in 1994 approved a measure allowing physician-aided suicide, but the statute has been tied up in court.
Oregon officials have raised the possibility that federal funds might be used to carry out the law if it takes effect.

Supporters of assisted suicide argue it can spare a terminally ill patient needless pain and agony. Opponents, including the American Medical Association and Catholic church, told Congress in recent testimony it is morally and ethically wrong to cause a patient's death intentionally.

Before approving the bill, lawmakers rejected an amendment by Ohio Representative Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, that would have required federally aided medical schools to teach pain management and other issues related to death and dying.
"The bill by itself really does nothing to alleviate the pain and treat the depression that leads terminally ill patients to contemplate suicide," said Brown.
The committee instead passed an alternative providing funding for research and development of such programmes and calling for a one-year government study into the issue.
"For us to mandate a curriculum that's already in the process says we don't trust the ... medical community to do the right thing," said Oklahoma Republican Tom Coburn.
Sponsors said the bill would not affect a seriously ill patient's right to refuse or discontinue medical treatment.

The bill clarifies that doctors may take actions that increase the risk of death, so long as they are not intended to end life. Such steps might include ending nutrition aid or the use of potent medication.
